title: Why suffering?
hook: the Qur'an promises tests, and tells a story about a wisdom that only shows up later

segments.voice: Yesterday, free will and decree, and your line: choose, and trust. Did you do the good thing you chose, and let the result go? Today, the question behind the trust. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

"And surely We shall try you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth and lives and crops; but give glad tidings to the steadfast." That's the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, and it doesn't promise an easy life. It promises tests: fear, hunger, loss. The next verse describes the steadfast. When misfortune strikes them, they say: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Muslims say that line at news of a death, a loss, a broken thing. The theologians of this part argued long about why a just and merciful God allows pain. Today, not a final answer, but what the Qur'an itself puts on the table.
screen: `WE SHALL TRY YOU.` → `FEAR, HUNGER, LOSS.` → `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an's clearest picture comes as a story, in Surah al-Kahf. The prophet Musa travels with a servant of Allah who has been given knowledge from Him. Tradition calls him al-Khidr. Musa asks to learn from him, and is warned he won't be able to bear it. Then three strange things happen. Al-Khidr makes a hole in the boat of some poor people who gave them a ride. He kills a boy. And in a town that refused them food, he rebuilds a falling wall and asks nothing for it. Each time Musa protests. Each time he's reminded of the warning. At the parting, al-Khidr explains. A king was seizing every boat by force; a damaged one might be passed over. The boy would have burdened his believing parents with rebellion and disbelief. The wall hid treasure belonging to two orphans, and it had to stand until they were grown. Everything Musa saw as harm had a purpose he couldn't see from where he stood. Another verse says it plainly: "Allah knoweth, ye know not." That doesn't make pain small, and Islam doesn't ask anyone to pretend it is. When the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ son Ibrahim was dying, Sahih al-Bukhari records that his eyes filled with tears. He said the eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. Tears, and trust, in the same breath. Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, says the believer's affair is all good: thankful in ease, patient in hardship, and both bring good. The hadith doesn't say every loss makes sense today. The story of the boat says the wisdom is not always seen.
screen: `A HOLE IN THE BOAT.` · `MUSA CAN'T SEE THE REASON.` · `TEARS, AND TRUST, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `ALLAH KNOWETH, YE KNOW NOT.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with a question honestly. Settle, and breathe. Let one hard thing come to mind, your own or someone else's. Not the hardest; one you can hold for two minutes. Don't try to explain it. Don't hurry to find the hidden reason. Just let the question sit there: why? If grief comes, let it come; the Prophet wept. Then, gently, add one more thought beside the question, without pushing the question away: I may not see all of it. If you pray, you can say the line from the verse: unto Him we are returning. The bell holds the time.
Why suffering? The Qur'an speaks of tests, of patience, and of a wisdom not always seen, told in the story of Musa and al-Khidr. Today's word.

Your line: not always seen. Today, when something goes wrong, leave a little room for a reason you can't see yet, and let yourself feel it too. Tomorrow, the attributes. Day one thousand two hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Muslims meet hardship with patience, sabr, and say "we are Allah's and unto Him we are returning" at news of a death or loss; grief and tears are not forbidden, and the Prophet himself wept.

fork.setup: you're Musa. your guide has just made a hole in the boat of the poor people who gave you a ride. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Musa protests, though he'd promised patience. Later he learns a king was seizing every boat by force, and a damaged one might be passed over.

trapdoor: what you thought: religion says suffering is always a punishment.
what it means: the Qur'an speaks of tests, patience, and a wisdom not always seen, without forbidding grief.
what a scholar hears: the Musa and al-Khidr story in Surah al-Kahf, and the theologians' long argument about justice and pain.
